rv.q: Grand Horizons is a sweet, sweet delight.

Bill and Nancy, the husband and wife at the heart of this new play by Bess Wohl, fall into the latter category. As Grand Horizons begins, they are performing a brittle pas de deux around the salt shaker in advance of what promises to be a mirthlessly taciturn dinner in a bland suburban retirement community.
Grand Horizons is not especially profound, and its women are written more fully than its men.
Bess Wohl's comedy-drama about a long-married couple who suddenly decide to divorce is elevated by Jane Alexander and James Cromwell's beautifully nuanced performances as the separating spouses.
For those few minutes, at least, Grand Horizons achieves a poignancy and depth that have otherwise eluded it.

Unfortunately, her realization that she can no longer tell the requisite wifely lies — the ones that say her husband and children are infinitely excusable — comes too late in her life, as too late in the play.
Bess Wohl's comedy about the breakup of a couple living in a senior community is humorous, but just barely.
"Grand Horizons" delivers old-fashioned entertainment that's become a rarity on Broadway.
The comedy and drama in Grand Horizons work in clever interplay.
It’s damn funny, and very on-point.
Back and forth the play goes—sometimes silly, sometimes deadly serious.
Best efforts and a sweet heart notwithstanding, Grand Horizons falls short of its expansive title.
With Grand Horizons, she seems to have wanted to step back and try her hand at a traditional, non-challenging, old-fashioned sex comedy.
But the play’s horizons are too easy and narrow.
